info.text: Public health protects communities by observing patterns, preventing harm, improving shared conditions, and coordinating responses when threats emerge.

clusters.name: Understand population health
clusters.fact: Public health combines reports, measurements, surveys, laboratory evidence, and vital records to identify patterns affecting communities rather than relying on isolated cases alone.

case reports.text: Reports describing identified cases of a disease or other health event.

disease rates.text: Measures that relate the number of health events to the size of the population in which they occur.

health surveys.text: Structured collection of health information from a sample or population.

laboratory results.text: Findings from tests used to detect pathogens, exposures, or other biological evidence.

mortality records.text: Records of deaths and their reported causes, used to study population patterns over time.

clusters.name: Prevent illness and injury
clusters.fact: Prevention reduces the chance that harm will occur, detects problems early, and lowers their consequences before treatment becomes the only remaining option.

vaccination.text: The administration of a vaccine to help the immune system prevent or reduce disease.

screening.text: Testing people without recognized symptoms to identify possible disease or risk early.

safer workplaces.text: Policies, engineering controls, training, and standards that reduce occupational illness and injury.

nutrition programs.text: Organized efforts that improve access to adequate food or support healthier dietary patterns.

injury prevention.text: Measures designed to reduce the likelihood or severity of injuries.

clusters.name: Protect shared environments
clusters.fact: Many public-health protections work upstream by making water, food, air, workplaces, and other shared surroundings safer for everyone who depends on them.

clean water.text: Water protected from contaminants through source protection, treatment, testing, and safe distribution.

food safety.text: Practices and controls that prevent foodborne illness and contamination.

air quality.text: The condition of outdoor or indoor air as shaped by pollutants and other exposures.

sanitation.text: Systems and practices for safely managing waste and maintaining hygienic conditions.

hazard regulation.text: Rules and enforcement intended to limit exposure to conditions or substances that can cause harm.

clusters.name: Prepare and respond
clusters.fact: Public-health response connects preparation, investigation, communication, logistics, and coordinated action so emerging threats can be contained and communities supported.

emergency planning.text: Advance preparation for roles, resources, communication, and operations during a health emergency.

outbreak investigation.text: The systematic effort to determine whether an outbreak exists, identify its source and spread, and guide control measures.

contact tracing.text: Identifying and notifying people who may have been exposed to an infectious disease.

public communication.text: Sharing timely, understandable information about risks, evidence, and recommended actions.

resource coordination.text: Organizing personnel, supplies, facilities, and partnerships so a response can reach affected communities.

bridges.fact: Surveillance turns continuing observation into actionable knowledge: reports and measurements are collected and interpreted so emerging threats can be detected, responses directed, and results evaluated.

info.text: The ongoing, systematic collection, analysis, interpretation, and sharing of health data for public-health action.

bridges.fact: Public health reduces risk through both targeted preventive services and changes to shared environments, recognizing that health depends on more than individual choices or medical treatment.

info.text: Measures that lower the probability or expected severity of harm.

bridges.fact: Evidence-based action uses population observations and research to choose preventive measures, while continuing to test whether those measures are effective, proportionate, and responsive to new evidence.

info.text: Using the best available evidence, together with context and professional judgment, to guide and evaluate public-health decisions.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts operate mainly at the level of communities or populations rather than one patient at a time?
lenses.explanation: These concepts reveal population patterns or change the conditions, information, and protections shared by many people at once.

reasons.disease rates: They summarize how often illness occurs across a defined population.
reasons.health surveys: They gather information from groups to reveal needs and disparities that individual encounters may miss.
reasons.clean water: It protects everyone who depends on a shared water system.
reasons.air quality: It describes a shared environmental exposure rather than one person's diagnosis.
reasons.public communication: It gives a population timely information for coordinated protective action.

lenses.prompt: Which protections may become least visible when they are working well?
lenses.explanation: Successful prevention often appears as an event that never happens: an infection avoided, an injury prevented, an exposure removed, or a response made ready before a crisis.

reasons.vaccination: Its success includes infections and complications that never occur.
reasons.safer workplaces: Effective safeguards prevent injuries that would otherwise make the danger visible.
reasons.clean water: Reliable treatment makes waterborne disease unusual enough to be forgotten.
reasons.food safety: Routine inspection and controls prevent outbreaks before consumers notice a problem.
reasons.emergency planning: Preparation is most successful when a later response looks orderly rather than improvised.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts primarily produce or communicate information used to guide public-health decisions?
lenses.explanation: Public health depends on information moving in both directions: observations are assembled into population knowledge, and findings are communicated so institutions and communities can act.

reasons.case reports: They provide observations about identified illnesses or health events.
reasons.disease rates: They turn counts into comparable measures across populations and time.
reasons.health surveys: They reveal experiences, behaviors, and conditions that clinical records alone cannot show.
reasons.laboratory results: They help identify pathogens, exposures, and biological evidence.
reasons.mortality records: They reveal patterns in causes of death across places, groups, and time.
reasons.public communication: It translates findings and recommendations into information people can use.
